title: Coding Agents with Environment Interaction: A Theoretical Perspective
summary: Coding agents are increasingly utilized in test-driven software development, yet the theoretical mechanisms behind their environment-interaction strategies remain underexplored. We provide a probabilistic framework for two dominant paradigms: code selection after generation using the execution environment, and code generation conditioned on environment feedback. First, we formalize several well-established selection heuristics as environment-aware estimators of code correctness. We theoretically prove that estimators based on fuzzy functional similarity add an inductive bias and strictly dominate estimators based on functional equivalence in terms of signal-to-noise ratio. Second, we frame backprompting as an in-context approximation of Thompson sampling. We derive a novel regret bound for reward functions with unobservable components, theoretically explaining why the effectiveness of backprompting is limited by the ambiguity of the informal task description (an irreducible regret). Using three state-of-the-art open weight models, we corroborate these findings across BigCodeBenchHard, LeetCodeDataset, and QiskitHumanEvalSim. Our formalization also suggests how to improve task descriptions effectively, leading to a new benchmark, QiskitHumanEvalSimX.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a probabilistic framework to understand how coding agents interact with execution environments, formalizing selection heuristics and backprompting, proving theoretical advantages of fuzzy similarity over exact matching, and introducing a new benchmark for improved task descriptions.
AI.motivation: The theoretical underpinnings of how coding agents use execution feedback are poorly understood, despite their widespread use in test-driven development; this work aims to formalize and analyze dominant strategies like code selection and backprompting.
AI.method: The authors model code selection as environment-aware estimation of correctness, proving signal-to-noise advantages of fuzzy functional similarity; they interpret backprompting as in-context Thompson sampling and derive a regret bound for reward functions with unobservable components; they validate findings on three code benchmarks using open-weight models.
AI.result: Fuzzy similarity-based estimators theoretically dominate equivalence-based ones in signal quality; backprompting's effectiveness is limited by task ambiguity, formalized as irreducible regret; empirical results across benchmarks confirm the theoretical analysis; improved task descriptions lead to the creation of QiskitHumanEvalSimX.
AI.conclusion: The proposed probabilistic framework provides theoretical justification for common practices in coding agents and identifies limits of current feedback mechanisms; it also offers actionable insights for improving task specifications and evaluation benchmarks.

title: Scaling Mobile Chaos Testing with AI-Driven Test Execution
comment: 10 pages of content, 1 page of citations, 7 figures, 6 tables
summary: Mobile applications in large-scale distributed systems are susceptible to backend service failures, yet traditional chaos engineering approaches cannot scale mobile testing due to the combinatorial explosion of flows, locations, and failure scenarios that need validation. We present an automated mobile chaos testing system that integrates DragonCrawl, an LLM-based mobile testing platform, with uHavoc, a service-level fault injection system. The key insight is that adaptive AI-driven test execution can navigate mobile applications under degraded backend conditions, eliminating the need to manually write test cases for each combination of user flow, city, and failure type. Since Q1 2024, our system has executed over 180,000 automated chaos tests across 47 critical flows in Uber's Rider, Driver, and Eats applications, representing approximately 39,000 hours of manual testing effort that would be impractical at this scale. We identified 23 resilience risks, with 70% being architectural dependency violations where non-critical service failures degraded core user flows. Twelve issues were severe enough to prevent trip requests or food orders. Two caused application crashes detectable only through mobile chaos testing, not backend testing alone. Automated root cause analysis reduced debugging time from hours to minutes, achieving 88% precision@5 in attributing mobile failures to specific backend services. This paper presents the system design, evaluates its performance under fault injection (maintaining 99% test reliability), and reports operational experience demonstrating that continuous mobile resilience validation is achievable at production scale.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an automated mobile chaos testing system that combines LLM-based testing (DragonCrawl) with backend fault injection (uHavoc) to enable scalable resilience validation across Uber's mobile apps, identifying critical failures and reducing debugging effort through AI-driven execution and root cause analysis.
AI.motivation: Traditional chaos engineering does not scale for mobile testing due to the combinatorial complexity of user flows, geographic locations, and failure modes, necessitating an automated approach to validate mobile application resilience in large-scale distributed systems.
AI.method: The authors integrate DragonCrawl, an LLM-based mobile testing platform, with uHavoc, a service-level fault injection system, to automate chaos testing across diverse user flows, locations, and failure scenarios. Adaptive AI-driven execution navigates mobile apps under backend degradation, while automated root cause analysis identifies fault sources with high precision.
AI.result: The system executed over 180,000 automated chaos tests across 47 critical flows in Uber's apps, saving ~39,000 manual testing hours. It identified 23 resilience risks, including 70% architectural dependency violations, 12 severe functional issues, and 2 crashes only detectable via mobile testing. Root cause analysis achieved 88% precision@5 and reduced debugging time from hours to minutes, with 99% test reliability under fault injection.
AI.conclusion: The presented automated mobile chaos testing system enables continuous, large-scale resilience validation in production environments by combining AI-driven test execution with service-level fault injection, demonstrating that manual testing limitations can be overcome with adaptive, intelligent systems.

title: Trustworthy AI Software Engineers
comment: The first three authors contributed equally to this work
summary: With the rapid rise of AI coding agents, the fundamental premise of what it means to be a software engineer is in question. In this vision paper, we re-examine what it means for an AI agent to be considered a software engineer and then critically think about what makes such an agent trustworthy. \textit{Grounded} in established definitions of software engineering (SE) and informed by recent research on agentic AI systems, we conceptualise AI software engineers as participants in human-AI SE teams composed of human software engineers and AI models and tools, and we distinguish trustworthiness as a key property of these systems and actors rather than a subjective human attitude. Based on historical perspectives and emerging visions, we identify key dimensions that contribute to the trustworthiness of AI software engineers, spanning technical quality, transparency and accountability, epistemic humility, and societal and ethical alignment. We further discuss how trustworthiness can be evaluated and demonstrated, highlighting a fundamental trust measurement gap: not everything that matters for trust can be easily measured. Finally, we outline implications for the design, evaluation, and governance of AI SE systems, advocating for an ethics-by-design approach to enable appropriate trust in future human-AI SE teams.

AI.tldr: This vision paper redefines AI agents as collaborative members of software engineering teams and emphasizes objective trustworthiness through technical, ethical, and societal dimensions, advocating for ethics-by-design in AI software engineering systems.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the increasing integration of AI coding agents into software engineering practices, prompting a re-evaluation of the role of software engineers and the need to ensure that AI agents are trustworthy participants in collaborative development environments.
AI.method: The paper uses a conceptual and reflective methodology, grounded in established definitions of software engineering and recent research on agentic AI, to define AI software engineers within human-AI teams and identify core dimensions of their trustworthiness.
AI.result: The paper identifies key dimensions of trustworthiness in AI software engineers—technical quality, transparency and accountability, epistemic humility, and societal and ethical alignment—and highlights a trust measurement gap where critical aspects of trust cannot be easily quantified.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that trustworthiness in AI software engineers should be treated as an essential, objective property rather than a subjective human perception, and calls for an ethics-by-design approach in the development, evaluation, and governance of AI software engineering systems to foster appropriate trust in human-AI teams.

title: Multi-Agent-Driven Cognitive Secure Communications in Satellite-Terrestrial Networks
summary: Satellite-terrestrial networks (STNs) have emerged as a promising architecture for providing seamless wireless coverage and connectivity for multiple users. However, potential malicious eavesdroppers pose a serious threat to the private information via STNs due to their non-cooperative behavior and ability to launch intelligent attacks. To address this challenge, we propose a cognitive secure communication framework driven by multiple agents that coordinates spectrum scheduling and protection through real-time sensing, thereby disrupting the judgment of eavesdroppers while preserving reliable data transmission. On this basis, we formulate an optimization problem to maximize the secrecy probability of legitimate users, subject to a reliable transmission probability threshold. To tackle this problem, we propose a two-layer coordinated defense system. First, we develop a foundation layer based on multi-agent coordination schedule to determine the satellite operation matrix and the frequency slot occupation matrices, aiming to mitigate spectrum congestion and enhance transmission reliability. Then, we exploit generative adversarial networks to produce adversarial matrices, and employ learning-aided power control to set real and adversarial signal powers for protection layer, which actively degrades the inference capability of eavesdroppers. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms benchmark methods in terms of enhancing security performance and reducing power overhead for STNs in the cognitive secure communication scenario.

AI.tldr: A cognitive secure communication framework using multi-agent coordination and generative adversarial networks is proposed to enhance secrecy probability and reduce power overhead in satellite-terrestrial networks.
AI.motivation: Secure communication in satellite-terrestrial networks is threatened by intelligent, non-cooperative eavesdroppers that can compromise private information, necessitating proactive and adaptive defense mechanisms.
AI.method: A two-layer coordinated defense system is proposed: 1) a foundation layer using multi-agent coordination for spectrum scheduling (satellite operation and frequency slot matrices) to reduce congestion and improve reliability; 2) a protection layer using generative adversarial networks to create adversarial matrices and learning-aided power control to optimize real and adversarial signal powers, degrading eavesdropper inference capabilities. An optimization problem is formulated to maximize secrecy probability under reliability constraints.
AI.result: Simulation results show the proposed method outperforms benchmarks in enhancing security (higher secrecy probability) and reducing power overhead while maintaining reliable transmission in cognitive satellite-terrestrial networks.
AI.conclusion: The integration of multi-agent coordination and adversarial learning enables robust, proactive defense against intelligent eavesdroppers, making the proposed framework effective for secure and efficient cognitive communication in satellite-terrestrial networks.

title: AgentStepper: Interactive Debugging of Software Development Agents
summary: Software development agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have shown great promise in automating tasks like environment setup, issue solving, and program repair. Unfortunately, understanding and debugging such agents remain challenging due to their complex and dynamic nature. Developers must reason about trajectories of LLM queries, tool calls, and code modifications, but current techniques reveal little of this intermediate process in a comprehensible format. The key insight of this paper is that debugging software development agents shares many similarities with conventional debugging of software programs, yet requires a higher level of abstraction that raises the level from low-level implementation details to high-level agent actions. Drawing on this insight, we introduce AgentStepper, the first interactive debugger for LLM-based software engineering agents. AgentStepper enables developers to inspect, control, and interactively manipulate agent trajectories. AgentStepper represents trajectories as structured conversations among an LLM, the agent program, and tools. It supports breakpoints, stepwise execution, and live editing of prompts and tool invocations, while capturing and displaying intermediate repository-level code changes. Our evaluation applies AgentStepper to three state-of-the-art software development agents, ExecutionAgent, SWE-Agent, and RepairAgent, showing that integrating the approach into existing agents requires minor code changes (39-42 edited lines). Moreover, we report on a user study with twelve participants, indicating that AgentStepper improves the ability of participants to interpret trajectories (64% vs. 67% mean performance) and identify bugs in the agent's implementation (17% vs. 60% success rate), while reducing perceived workload (e.g., frustration reduced from 5.4/7.0 to 2.4/7.0) compared to conventional tools.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AgentStepper, the first interactive debugger for LLM-based software development agents, enabling stepwise control, inspection, and modification of agent behavior through high-level, structured trajectory visualization, resulting in substantially improved debugging performance and reduced cognitive load.
AI.motivation: Debugging LLM-based software development agents is difficult due to their complex, dynamic behaviors and the lack of transparent, high-level representations of their execution trajectories, which hinders effective analysis and troubleshooting.
AI.method: The authors designed AgentStepper, an interactive debugger that models agent executions as structured conversations among the LLM, agent program, and tools, enabling breakpoints, stepwise execution, live editing of prompts and tool calls, and visualization of code changes at the repository level.
AI.result: AgentStepper was integrated into three state-of-the-art agents with minimal code changes (39–42 lines) and evaluated in a user study with twelve participants, showing improved trajectory interpretation (64% vs. 67% mean performance), higher bug identification success (17% vs. 60%), and reduced perceived workload and frustration (from 5.4 to 2.4 on a 7-point scale).
AI.conclusion: AgentStepper significantly improves developers' ability to understand, debug, and interact with LLM-based software development agents by providing an interactive, high-level debugging interface that captures and visualizes agent trajectories effectively.

title: Know Your Scientist: KYC as Biosecurity Infrastructure
summary: Biological AI tools for protein design and structure prediction are advancing rapidly, creating dual-use risks that existing safeguards cannot adequately address. Current model-level restrictions, including keyword filtering, output screening, and content-based access denials, are fundamentally ill-suited to biology, where reliable function prediction remains beyond reach and novel threats evade detection by design. We propose a three-tier Know Your Customer (KYC) framework, inspired by anti-money laundering (AML) practices in the financial sector, that shifts governance from content inspection to user verification and monitoring. Tier I leverages research institutions as trust anchors to vouch for affiliated researchers and assume responsibility for vetting. Tier II applies output screening through sequence homology searches and functional annotation. Tier III monitors behavioral patterns to detect anomalies inconsistent with declared research purposes. This layered approach preserves access for legitimate researchers while raising the cost of misuse through institutional accountability and traceability. The framework can be implemented immediately using existing institutional infrastructure, requiring no new legislation or regulatory mandates.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Know Your Customer (KYC) framework for biological AI, using institutional verification and behavioral monitoring to mitigate dual-use risks in protein design and structure prediction, offering a feasible, immediate governance solution without new regulations.
AI.motivation: Rapid advances in biological AI tools for protein design and structure prediction pose significant dual-use risks that current content-based safeguards are unable to effectively address due to the complexity and unpredictability of biological functions.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-tier Know Your Customer (KYC) framework adapted from anti-money laundering practices, with Tier I relying on institutional vetting, Tier II employing sequence homology and functional annotation for output screening, and Tier III implementing behavioral monitoring to detect anomalous usage patterns.
AI.result: The KYC framework enables effective governance by shifting focus from unreliable content inspection to verifiable user identity and behavior, enhancing traceability and accountability while maintaining accessibility for legitimate scientific work.
AI.conclusion: The proposed three-tier KYC framework offers a practical and immediate solution for governing biological AI tools by emphasizing user verification and institutional accountability, thereby mitigating dual-use risks without restricting legitimate research.

title: Code vs Serialized AST Inputs for LLM-Based Code Summarization: An Empirical Study
comment: Accepted at the 3rd International Workshop on Large Language Models for Code (LLM4Code 2026), co-located with ICSE 2026
summary: Summarizing source code into natural language descriptions (code summarization) helps developers better understand program functionality and reduce the burden of software maintenance. Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), as opposed to source code, have been shown to improve summarization quality in traditional encoder-decoder-based code summarization models. However, most large language model (LLM)-based code summarization methods rely on raw code or only incorporate partial AST signals, meaning that the potential of complete AST representation has not been fully explored for LLMs. This paper presents AST(NIT), an AST augmentation and serialization method that preserves lexical details and encodes structural information into LLM-compatible sequences. Experiments with the LLaMA-3.1-8B model on the CodeXGLUE Python dataset show that the proposed serialized ASTs reduce the length of LLM inputs, require shorter training times, and achieve summarization quality comparable to existing approaches.

AI.tldr: AST(NIT) is an AST serialization method for code summarization that enhances LLM input efficiency by preserving lexical and structural information, yielding comparable performance with reduced input size and training time.
AI.motivation: To fully exploit the structural information of Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) in LLM-based code summarization, addressing the limitation of current methods that use raw code or partial AST signals.
AI.method: AST(NIT), an AST augmentation and serialization technique that preserves lexical information and encodes structural details into sequences compatible with large language models.
AI.result: Using LLaMA-3.1-8B on the CodeXGLUE Python dataset, AST(NIT) reduces input length and training time while achieving summarization quality on par with existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AST(NIT) method effectively leverages complete AST representations for LLM-based code summarization, demonstrating efficiency and competitiveness in performance.

title: Identifying Adversary Tactics and Techniques in Malware Binaries with an LLM Agent
summary: Understanding TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) in malware binaries is essential for security analysis and threat intelligence, yet remains challenging in practice. Real-world malware binaries are typically stripped of symbols, contain large numbers of functions, and distribute malicious behavior across multiple code regions, making TTP attribution difficult. Recent large language models (LLMs) offer strong code understanding capabilities, but applying them directly to this task faces challenges in identifying analysis entry points, reasoning under partial observability, and misalignment with TTP-specific decision logic. We present TTPDetect, the first LLM agent for recognizing TTPs in stripped malware binaries. TTPDetect combines dense retrieval with LLM-based neural retrieval to narrow the space of analysis entry points. TTPDetect further employs a function-level analyzing agent consisting of a Context Explorer that performs on-demand, incremental context retrieval and a TTP-Specific Reasoning Guideline that achieves inference-time alignment. We build a new dataset that labels decompiled functions with TTPs across diverse malware families and platforms. TTPDetect achieves 93.25% precision and 93.81% recall on function-level TTP recognition, outperforming baselines by 10.38% and 18.78%, respectively. When evaluated on real world malware samples, TTPDetect recognizes TTPs with a precision of 87.37%. For malware with expert-written reports, TTPDetect recovers 85.7% of the documented TTPs and further discovers, on average, 10.5 previously unreported TTPs per malware.

AI.tldr: TTPDetect is the first LLM agent designed to identify Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) in stripped malware binaries by combining dense and neural retrieval to pinpoint analysis entry points, using a context-aware function-level agent with a Context Explorer and TTP-specific reasoning, achieving high precision and recall on both labeled data and real-world samples.
AI.motivation: Identifying TTPs in real-world malware is difficult due to stripped symbols, numerous functions, and distributed malicious logic; existing LLMs struggle with entry point identification, partial observability, and misalignment with TTP reasoning.
AI.method: TTPDetect uses hybrid retrieval (dense + LLM-based) to identify entry points, employs a function-level agent with a Context Explorer for incremental context gathering, and introduces a TTP-Specific Reasoning Guideline for inference-time alignment; evaluation is performed on a new dataset with function-level TTP annotations across diverse malware.
AI.result: TTPDetect achieves 93.25% precision and 93.81% recall on function-level TTP recognition, outperforming baselines by 10.38% and 18.78%; on real malware, it reaches 87.37% precision, recovers 85.7% of expert-reported TTPs, and discovers an average of 10.5 new TTPs per sample.
AI.conclusion: TTPDetect effectively bridges the gap between LLMs and practical malware analysis by enabling accurate, context-aware TTP attribution in stripped binaries, demonstrating strong performance and utility in real-world threat intelligence.

title: Using Large Language Models to Support Automation of Failure Management in CI/CD Pipelines: A Case Study in SAP HANA
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of SANER 2026
summary: CI/CD pipeline failure management is time-consuming when performed manually. Automating this process is non-trivial because the information required for effective failure management is unstructured and cannot be automatically processed by traditional programs. With their ability to process unstructured data, large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results for automated failure management by previous work. Following these studies, we evaluated whether an LLM-based system could automate failure management in a CI/CD pipeline in the context of a large industrial software project, namely SAP HANA. We evaluated the ability of the LLM-based system to identify the error location and to propose exact solutions that contain no unnecessary actions. To support the LLM in generating exact solutions, we provided it with different types of domain knowledge, including pipeline information, failure management instructions, and data from historical failures. We conducted an ablation study to determine which type of domain knowledge contributed most to solution accuracy. The results show that data from historical failures contributed the most to the system's accuracy, enabling it to produce exact solutions in 92.1% of cases in our dataset. The system correctly identified the error location with 97.4% accuracy when provided with domain knowledge, compared to 84.2% accuracy without it. In conclusion, our findings indicate that LLMs, when provided with data from historical failures, represent a promising approach for automating CI/CD pipeline failure management.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates an LLM-based system for automating CI/CD pipeline failure management in SAP HANA. By leveraging domain knowledge—especially historical failure data—the system achieves high accuracy in error localization (97.4%) and exact solution generation (92.1%), demonstrating the effectiveness of LLMs in industrial software engineering automation.
AI.motivation: Manual CI/CD pipeline failure management is labor-intensive and inefficient. Traditional automation approaches struggle with unstructured data, motivating the use of LLMs capable of processing such information to improve automation accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: An LLM-based system was developed and evaluated to automate CI/CD pipeline failure management. The system was provided with various types of domain knowledge—pipeline information, failure management instructions, and historical failure data. An ablation study was conducted to assess the impact of each knowledge type on performance.
AI.result: The LLM-based system achieved 97.4% accuracy in identifying error locations when domain knowledge was provided, compared to 84.2% without it. Exact solution generation reached 92.1% accuracy, with historical failure data proving to be the most impactful knowledge source.
AI.conclusion: LLMs, when augmented with historical failure data, show strong potential for automating CI/CD pipeline failure management in large-scale industrial projects like SAP HANA, significantly improving accuracy in error localization and solution generation.

title: AdFL: In-Browser Federated Learning for Online Advertisement
summary: Since most countries are coming up with online privacy regulations, such as GDPR in the EU, online publishers need to find a balance between revenue from targeted advertisement and user privacy. One way to be able to still show targeted ads, based on user personal and behavioral information, is to employ Federated Learning (FL), which performs distributed learning across users without sharing user raw data with other stakeholders in the publishing ecosystem. This paper presents AdFL, an FL framework that works in the browsers to learn user ad preferences. These preferences are aggregated in a global FL model, which is then used in the browsers to show more relevant ads to users. AdFL can work with any model that uses features available in the browser such as ad viewability, ad click-through, user dwell time on pages, and page content. The AdFL server runs at the publisher and coordinates the learning process for the users who browse pages on the publisher's website. The AdFL prototype does not require the client to install any software, as it is built utilizing standard APIs available on most modern browsers. We built a proof-of-concept model for ad viewability prediction that runs on top of AdFL. We tested AdFL and the model with two non-overlapping datasets from a website with 40K visitors per day. The experiments demonstrate AdFL's feasibility to capture the training information in the browser in a few milliseconds, show that the ad viewability prediction achieves up to 92.59% AUC, and indicate that utilizing differential privacy (DP) to safeguard local model parameters yields adequate performance, with only modest declines in comparison to the non-DP variant.

AI.tldr: AdFL is a browser-based federated learning framework enabling privacy-preserving targeted advertising by training on user behavior locally and aggregating model updates server-side, achieving high ad viewability prediction accuracy while complying with privacy regulations.
AI.motivation: The need to comply with online privacy regulations like GDPR while maintaining effective targeted advertising motivates the development of privacy-preserving ad systems that avoid direct collection of user data.
AI.method: AdFL employs federated learning to train models directly in users' browsers using behavioral features (e.g., ad click-through, dwell time, page content) without sharing raw data. A central server at the publisher orchestrates model aggregation and distribution. The system uses standard web APIs and integrates differential privacy to protect model updates.
AI.result: AdFL successfully captures training data in milliseconds per user. The ad viewability prediction model achieves up to 92.59% AUC. With differential privacy, performance remains high with only minor degradation compared to the non-DP version.
AI.conclusion: AdFL is a feasible and practical framework for targeted advertising that balances user privacy and revenue generation by leveraging federated learning in browsers, with strong performance even when incorporating differential privacy.

title: Statistical-Based Metric Threshold Setting Method for Software Fault Prediction in Firmware Projects: An Industrial Experience
summary: Ensuring software quality in embedded firmware is critical, especially in safety-critical domains where compliance with functional safety standards (ISO 26262) requires strong guarantees of software reliability. While machine learning-based fault prediction models have demonstrated high accuracy, their lack of interpretability limits their adoption in industrial settings. Developers need actionable insights that can be directly employed in software quality assurance processes and guide defect mitigation strategies. In this paper, we present a structured process for defining context-specific software metric thresholds suitable for integration into fault detection workflows in industrial settings. Our approach supports cross-project fault prediction by deriving thresholds from one set of projects and applying them to independently developed firmware, thereby enabling reuse across similar software systems without retraining or domain-specific tuning. We analyze three real-world C-embedded firmware projects provided by an industrial partner, using Coverity and Understand static analysis tools to extract software metrics. Through statistical analysis and hypothesis testing, we identify discriminative metrics and derived empirical threshold values capable of distinguishing faulty from non-faulty functions. The derived thresholds are validated through an experimental evaluation, demonstrating their effectiveness in identifying fault-prone functions with high precision. The results confirm that the derived thresholds can serve as an interpretable solution for fault prediction, aligning with industry standards and SQA practices. This approach provides a practical alternative to black-box AI models, allowing developers to systematically assess software quality, take preventive actions, and integrate metric-based fault prediction into industrial development workflows to mitigate software faults.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an interpretable, threshold-based fault prediction method for embedded firmware using static analysis metrics, validated on three industrial C projects, enabling cross-project fault detection without retraining and supporting integration into safety-critical software development workflows.
AI.motivation: The lack of interpretability in machine learning-based fault prediction models hinders their adoption in safety-critical embedded systems, where compliance with standards like ISO 26262 demands transparent and actionable fault detection mechanisms.
AI.method: A structured process was developed to derive context-specific software metric thresholds from static analysis data (using Coverity and Understand tools) across three real-world C-embedded firmware projects. Discriminative metrics were identified through statistical analysis and hypothesis testing, and thresholds were validated via experimental evaluation for cross-project fault prediction without retraining.
AI.result: Empirical thresholds were successfully derived and validated, demonstrating high precision in identifying fault-prone functions. The method enabled effective cross-project fault prediction without domain-specific tuning or model retraining, supporting reuse across similar firmware systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides an interpretable, threshold-based method for fault prediction in embedded firmware that aligns with industrial software quality assurance practices and functional safety standards, offering a practical alternative to black-box AI models.

title: Zero-Trust Runtime Verification for Agentic Payment Protocols: Mitigating Replay and Context-Binding Failures in AP2
summary:
The deployment of autonomous AI agents capable of executing commercial transactions has motivated the adoption of mandate-based payment authorization protocols, including the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2). These protocols replace interactive, session-based authorization with cryptographically issued mandates, enabling asynchronous and autonomous execution. While AP2 provides specification-level guarantees through signature verification, explicit binding, and expiration semantics, real-world agentic execution introduces runtime behaviors such as retries, concurrency, and orchestration that challenge implicit assumptions about mandate usage.
  In this work, we present a security analysis of the AP2 mandate lifecycle and identify enforcement gaps that arise during runtime in agent-based payment systems. We propose a zero-trust runtime verification framework that enforces explicit context binding and consume-once mandate semantics using dynamically generated, time-bound nonces, ensuring that authorization decisions are evaluated at execution time rather than assumed from static issuance properties.
  Through simulation-based evaluation under high concurrency, we show that context-aware binding and consume-once enforcement address distinct and complementary attack classes, and that both are required to prevent replay and context-redirect attacks. The proposed framework mitigates all evaluated attacks while maintaining stable verification latency of approximately 3.8~ms at throughput levels up to 10{,}000 transactions per second. We further demonstrate that the required runtime state is bounded by peak concurrency rather than cumulative transaction history, indicating that robust runtime security for agentic payment execution can be achieved with minimal and predictable overhead.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes security gaps in the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) during runtime in autonomous agent systems and proposes a zero-trust framework using time-bound nonces to enforce context binding and single-use mandates, preventing replay and context-redirect attacks with low overhead and high throughput.
AI.motivation: Runtime behaviors in autonomous agent systems—such as retries, concurrency, and orchestration—introduce security risks that challenge the implicit assumptions of mandate-based payment protocols like AP2, necessitating runtime enforcement beyond static cryptographic guarantees.
AI.method: A zero-trust runtime verification framework is proposed, utilizing dynamically generated, time-bound nonces to enforce explicit context binding and consume-once mandate semantics. Evaluation is conducted via simulation under high concurrency to assess security and performance.
AI.result: The framework effectively mitigates replay and context-redirect attacks, with stable verification latency of ~3.8 ms at up to 10,000 transactions per second. Runtime state is bounded by peak concurrency, not transaction history, ensuring scalability and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Robust runtime security for agentic payment execution can be achieved with minimal and predictable overhead by enforcing context-aware binding and consume-once semantics using a zero-trust verification framework.

title: TraceCoder: A Trace-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Debugging of LLM-Generated Code
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate code with subtle but critical bugs, especially for complex tasks. Existing automated repair methods typically rely on superficial pass/fail signals, offering limited visibility into program behavior and hindering precise error localization. In addition, without a way to learn from prior failures, repair processes often fall into repetitive and inefficient cycles. To overcome these challenges, we present TraceCoder, a collaborative multi-agent framework that emulates the observe-analyze-repair process of human experts. The framework first instruments the code with diagnostic probes to capture fine-grained runtime traces, enabling deep insight into its internal execution. It then conducts causal analysis on these traces to accurately identify the root cause of the failure. This process is further enhanced by a novel Historical Lesson Learning Mechanism (HLLM), which distills insights from prior failed repair attempts to inform subsequent correction strategies and prevent recurrence of similar mistakes. To ensure stable convergence, a Rollback Mechanism enforces that each repair iteration constitutes a strict improvement toward the correct solution. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that TraceCoder achieves up to a 34.43\% relative improvement in Pass@1 accuracy over existing advanced baselines. Ablation studies verify the significance of each system component, with the iterative repair process alone contributing a 65.61\% relative gain in accuracy. Furthermore, TraceCoder significantly outperforms leading iterative methods in terms of both accuracy and cost-efficiency.

AI.tldr: TraceCoder is a multi-agent framework that improves code repair in LLMs by using runtime tracing, causal analysis, and learning from past failures, achieving up to 34.43% better Pass@1 accuracy than state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: LLMs frequently produce buggy code for complex tasks, and existing repair methods rely on coarse pass/fail feedback, limiting error localization and leading to repetitive, inefficient repair attempts due to lack of memory or learning from prior failures.
AI.method: TraceCoder employs a collaborative multi-agent system that (1) instruments code with diagnostic probes to collect fine-grained runtime traces, (2) performs causal analysis on traces to pinpoint root causes, (3) uses a Historical Lesson Learning Mechanism (HLLM) to distill knowledge from past failures, and (4) applies a Rollback Mechanism to ensure only beneficial changes are retained during iterative repair.
AI.result: TraceCoder achieves up to 34.43% relative improvement in Pass@1 accuracy across multiple benchmarks. Ablation studies show the iterative repair process contributes a 65.61% relative accuracy gain, and the system outperforms leading methods in both accuracy and cost-efficiency.
AI.conclusion: By integrating runtime observation, causal diagnosis, and memory-driven learning, TraceCoder effectively enhances code repair in LLMs, enabling precise error correction and efficient convergence while avoiding recurring mistakes.

title: VENOMREC: Cross-Modal Interactive Poisoning for Targeted Promotion in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are pushing recommender systems (RecSys) toward content-grounded retrieval and ranking via cross-modal fusion. We find that while cross-modal consensus often mitigates conventional poisoning that manipulates interaction logs or perturbs a single modality, it also introduces a new attack surface where synchronised multimodal poisoning can reliably steer fused representations along stable semantic directions during fine-tuning. To characterise this threat, we formalise cross-modal interactive poisoning and propose VENOMREC, which performs Exposure Alignment to identify high-exposure regions in the joint embedding space and Cross-modal Interactive Perturbation to craft attention-guided coupled token-patch edits. Experiments on three real-world multimodal datasets demonstrate that VENOMREC consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving 0.73 mean ER@20 and improving over the strongest baseline by +0.52 absolute ER points on average, while maintaining comparable recommendation utility.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a new security threat in multimodal recommender systems where synchronized text-image poisoning can exploit cross-modal fusion; it proposes VENOMREC, a novel attack method using exposure-aligned, attention-guided perturbations that effectively manipulates recommendations with minimal detection risk.
AI.motivation: While cross-modal fusion in multimodal recommender systems improves robustness against single-modality attacks, it introduces a new vulnerability to synchronized multimodal poisoning that can subtly and consistently manipulate model behavior through aligned perturbations.
AI.method: VENOMREC employs Exposure Alignment to detect high-exposure regions in the joint embedding space and uses Cross-modal Interactive Perturbation to generate attention-guided, coupled token-patch modifications in text and image modalities for coordinated poisoning.
AI.result: VENOMREC significantly outperforms strong baselines across three real-world multimodal datasets, achieving a mean ER@20 of 0.73 and an average improvement of +0.52 ER points over the best baseline, while maintaining comparable recommendation performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed VENOMREC framework effectively exploits the vulnerability of cross-modal consensus in multimodal recommender systems, demonstrating that synchronized multimodal poisoning can reliably manipulate fused representations during fine-tuning while preserving recommendation utility.

title: Beyond Function-Level Analysis: Context-Aware Reasoning for Inter-Procedural Vulnerability Detection
summary:
Recent progress in ML and LLMs has improved vulnerability detection, and recent datasets have reduced label noise and unrelated code changes. However, most existing approaches still operate at the function level, where models are asked to predict whether a single function is vulnerable without inter-procedural context. In practice, vulnerability presence and root cause often depend on contextual information. Naively appending such context is not a reliable solution: real-world context is long, redundant, and noisy, and we find that unstructured context frequently degrades the performance of strong fine-tuned code models.
  We present CPRVul, a context-aware vulnerability detection framework that couples Context Profiling and Selection with Structured Reasoning. CPRVul constructs a code property graph, and extracts candidate context. It then uses an LLM to generate security-focused profiles and assign relevance scores, selecting only high-impact contextual elements that fit within the model's context window. In the second phase, CPRVul integrates the target function, the selected context, and auxiliary vulnerability metadata to generate reasoning traces, which are used to fine-tune LLMs for reasoning-based vulnerability detection.
  We evaluate CPRVul on three high-quality vulnerability datasets: PrimeVul, TitanVul, and CleanVul. Across all datasets, CPRVul consistently outperforms function-only baselines, achieving accuracies ranging from 64.94% to 73.76%, compared to 56.65% to 63.68% for UniXcoder. Specifically, on the challenging PrimeVul benchmark, CPRVul achieves 67.78% accuracy, outperforming prior state-of-the-art approaches, improving accuracy from 55.17% to 67.78% (22.9% improvement). Our ablations further show that neither raw context nor processed context alone benefits strong code models; gains emerge only when processed context is paired with structured reasoning.

AI.tldr: CPRVul is a context-aware vulnerability detection framework that improves upon function-level methods by using context profiling, selection, and structured reasoning to incorporate relevant inter-procedural information, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Vulnerabilities often depend on inter-procedural context, but existing methods either ignore context or degrade performance when using raw, noisy context. There is a need for selective and structured use of context in vulnerability detection.
AI.method: CPRVul builds a code property graph to extract candidate context, uses an LLM to profile and score context relevance, selects high-impact context within the model's window, and employs structured reasoning traces (target function + selected context + metadata) to fine-tune LLMs for detection.
AI.result: CPRVul outperforms function-only baselines across PrimeVul, TitanVul, and CleanVul datasets, achieving 64.94%–73.76% accuracy vs. 56.65%–63.68% for UniXcoder. On PrimeVul, it reaches 67.78% accuracy (22.9% improvement over prior SOTA). Ablations show gains require both processed context and structured reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Effective vulnerability detection requires not just more context, but intelligently selected and structured context combined with reasoning-aware training; CPRVul demonstrates that this approach significantly boosts performance over existing methods.

title: The Avatar Cache: Enabling On-Demand Security with Morphable Cache Architecture
summary: The sharing of the last-level cache (LLC) among multiple cores makes it vulnerable to cross-core conflict- and occupancy-based attacks. Despite extensive prior work, modern processors still employ non-secure set-associative LLCs. Existing secure LLC designs broadly fall into two categories: (i) randomized and (ii) partitioned. The state-of-the-art randomized design, Mirage, mitigates conflict-based attacks but incurs significant area overhead (20% additional storage) and design complexity. Partitioned LLCs mitigate both conflict- and occupancy-based attacks, but often suffer from large performance overheads (on average over 5% and up to 49%), require OS support in set-based schemes, or face scalability issues in way-based schemes. These factors pose major obstacles to the industrial adoption of secure LLCs. This paper asks whether strong LLC security can be achieved with minimal changes to a conventional set-associative LLC, enabling security only when needed while preserving low performance, power, and area overheads. We propose Avatar, a secure and morphable LLC that supports three modes: non-secure (Avatar-N), randomized secure (Avatar-R), and partitioned secure (Avatar-P), and can switch dynamically between them. Avatar closely resembles a conventional set-associative LLC, facilitating industrial adoption. Avatar-R introduces extra invalid entries and leverages high associativity to provide a strong security guarantee with little capacity loss, achieving only one set-associative eviction per $10^{30}$ years, while incurring 1.5% storage overhead, a 2.7% increase in static power, and a 0.2% slowdown over a 16~MB baseline. Avatar-P mitigates both conflict- and occupancy-based attacks with only a 3% performance overhead, substantially outperforming prior way-based partitioned LLCs. When security is unnecessary, Avatar switches to Avatar-N to maximize performance and energy efficiency.

AI.tldr: Avatar is a morphable last-level cache that dynamically switches between secure and non-secure modes, providing strong protection against conflict- and occupancy-based side-channel attacks with minimal overhead, enabling practical and efficient security in modern processors.
AI.motivation: Modern LLCs are vulnerable to cross-core attacks; existing secure designs suffer from high overheads or complexity, limiting industrial adoption. There is a need for a secure LLC that minimizes changes to conventional designs and enables on-demand security.
AI.method: Design and evaluation of Avatar, a morphable LLC supporting three operational modes (non-secure, randomized secure, and partitioned secure), leveraging invalid entries and high associativity for security with minimal performance and area impact.
AI.result: Avatar-R provides strong conflict-based attack resistance with 1.5% storage overhead, 2.7% increase in static power, and 0.2% performance slowdown. Avatar-P reduces performance overhead to 3%, significantly better than prior partitioned designs. Security can be disabled (Avatar-N) for optimal efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Avatar enables strong LLC security with minimal modifications to conventional set-associative caches, offering dynamic switching between secure and non-secure modes, low overhead, and improved practicality for industrial adoption.

title: TrajAD: Trajectory Anomaly Detection for Trustworthy LLM Agents
summary: We address the problem of runtime trajectory anomaly detection, a critical capability for enabling trustworthy LLM agents. Current safety measures predominantly focus on static input/output filtering. However, we argue that ensuring LLM agents reliability requires auditing the intermediate execution process. In this work, we formulate the task of Trajectory Anomaly Detection. The goal is not merely detection, but precise error localization. This capability is essential for enabling efficient rollback-and-retry. To achieve this, we construct TrajBench, a dataset synthesized via a perturb-and-complete strategy to cover diverse procedural anomalies. Using this benchmark, we investigate the capability of models in process supervision. We observe that general-purpose LLMs, even with zero-shot prompting, struggle to identify and localize these anomalies. This reveals that generalized capabilities do not automatically translate to process reliability. To address this, we propose TrajAD, a specialized verifier trained with fine-grained process supervision. Our approach outperforms baselines, demonstrating that specialized supervision is essential for building trustworthy agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Trajectory Anomaly Detection (TrajAD) for identifying and localizing runtime errors in LLM agents' execution processes, proposing a new benchmark (TrajBench) and a specialized verifier trained with fine-grained supervision to improve agent reliability.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety mechanisms rely on static input/output filtering, which cannot ensure reliability during dynamic execution; thus, there is a need to audit intermediate steps for trustworthy agent behavior.
AI.method: The authors formulate trajectory anomaly detection with error localization, create TrajBench using a perturb-and-complete strategy to generate procedural anomalies, and propose TrajAD—a specialized verifier trained with fine-grained process supervision—to detect and localize anomalies.
AI.result: Experiments show that general-purpose LLMs fail at zero-shot anomaly localization; TrajAD significantly outperforms baselines on TrajBench, demonstrating the necessity of specialized training for process reliability.
AI.conclusion: Specialized process supervision via fine-grained annotations is essential for enabling reliable and trustworthy LLM agents, surpassing general-purpose models in runtime anomaly detection and localization.

title: Subgraph Reconstruction Attacks on Graph RAG Deployments with Practical Defenses
summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (Graph RAG) is increasingly deployed to support LLM applications by augmenting user queries with structured knowledge retrieved from a knowledge graph. While Graph RAG improves relational reasoning, it introduces a largely understudied threat: adversaries can reconstruct subgraphs from a target RAG system's knowledge graph, enabling privacy inference and replication of curated knowledge assets. We show that existing attacks are largely ineffective against Graph RAG even with simple prompt-based safeguards, because these attacks expose explicit exfiltration intent and are therefore easily suppressed by lightweight safe prompts. We identify three technical challenges for practical Graph RAG extraction under realistic safeguards and introduce GRASP, a closed-box, multi-turn subgraph reconstruction attack. GRASP (i) reframes extraction as a context-processing task, (ii) enforces format-compliant, instance-grounded outputs via per-record identifiers to reduce hallucinations and preserve relational details, and (iii) diversifies goal-driven attack queries using a momentum-aware scheduler to operate within strict query budgets. Across two real-world knowledge graphs, four safety-aligned LLMs, and multiple Graph RAG frameworks, GRASP attains the strongest type-faithful reconstruction where prior methods fail, reaching up to 82.9 F1. We further evaluate defenses and propose two lightweight mitigations that substantially reduce reconstruction fidelity without utility loss.

AI.tldr: This paper presents GRASP, a stealthy, multi-turn attack that effectively reconstructs subgraphs from Graph RAG systems despite safety prompts, by using context-aware querying, output grounding, and query diversification; it achieves high reconstruction accuracy and proposes effective lightweight countermeasures.
AI.motivation: While Graph RAG enhances relational reasoning in LLMs by leveraging structured knowledge, it poses a privacy risk: adversarial subgraph reconstruction can lead to leakage of sensitive or proprietary knowledge. Existing attacks are ineffective due to explicit exfiltration patterns that trigger prompt-based safeguards, necessitating a more stealthy and robust approach.
AI.method: The authors introduce GRASP, a closed-box, multi-turn attack method that reframes extraction as a context-processing task. Key technical components include format-compliant, instance-grounded outputs using per-record identifiers to minimize hallucinations, and a momentum-aware scheduler to diversify queries and operate within limited query budgets.
AI.result: GRASP achieves up to 82.9 F1 score in type-faithful subgraph reconstruction across two real-world knowledge graphs, four safety-aligned LLMs, and multiple Graph RAG frameworks—outperforming prior methods where they fail. Evaluation of proposed defenses shows they significantly reduce attack success without degrading system performance.
AI.conclusion: GRASP represents a significant advancement in subgraph reconstruction attacks on Graph RAG systems, demonstrating high efficacy even under realistic safety constraints. The paper concludes by proposing two lightweight defenses that reduce reconstruction fidelity without impairing system utility.

title: Sequential Auditing for f-Differential Privacy
summary: We present new auditors to assess Differential Privacy (DP) of an algorithm based on output samples. Such empirical auditors are common to check for algorithmic correctness and implementation bugs. Most existing auditors are batch-based or targeted toward the traditional notion of $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP; typically both. In this work, we shift the focus to the highly expressive privacy concept of $f$-DP, in which the entire privacy behavior is captured by a single tradeoff curve. Our auditors detect violations across the full privacy spectrum with statistical significance guarantees, which are supported by theory and simulations. Most importantly, and in contrast to prior work, our auditors do not require a user-specified sample size as an input. Rather, they adaptively determine a near-optimal number of samples needed to reach a decision, thereby avoiding the excessively large sample sizes common in many auditing studies. This reduction in sampling cost becomes especially beneficial for expensive training procedures such as DP-SGD. Our method supports both whitebox and blackbox settings and can also be executed in single-run frameworks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces adaptive auditors for f-Differential Privacy that efficiently detect privacy violations using minimal samples without user input on sample size, improving practicality for costly training processes like DP-SGD.
AI.motivation: Existing DP auditors are often limited to batch processing and (ε,δ)-DP, requiring large, user-specified sample sizes; this work addresses the need for more expressive, efficient, and automated auditing for the richer f-DP framework.
AI.method: The authors develop adaptive, sample-efficient auditors for f-Differential Privacy that operate by analyzing output samples of an algorithm; these auditors work in both whitebox and blackbox settings and support single-run execution, using statistical methods to determine a near-optimal number of samples for decision-making.
AI.result: The proposed auditors achieve statistically sound privacy validation across the full f-DP spectrum with significantly reduced sample complexity, demonstrated through theoretical analysis and simulations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed auditors for f-DP offer adaptive, statistically significant detection of privacy violations across the entire privacy spectrum without requiring a pre-specified sample size, making them efficient and practical for real-world applications such as DP-SGD.

title: Dependable Artificial Intelligence with Reliability and Security (DAIReS): A Unified Syndrome Decoding Approach for Hallucination and Backdoor Trigger Detection
summary: Machine Learning (ML) models, including Large Language Models (LLMs), are characterized by a range of system-level attributes such as security and reliability. Recent studies have demonstrated that ML models are vulnerable to multiple forms of security violations, among which backdoor data-poisoning attacks represent a particularly insidious threat, enabling unauthorized model behavior and systematic misclassification. In parallel, deficiencies in model reliability can manifest as hallucinations in LLMs, leading to unpredictable outputs and substantial risks for end users. In this work on Dependable Artificial Intelligence with Reliability and Security (DAIReS), we propose a novel unified approach based on Syndrome Decoding for the detection of both security and reliability violations in learning-based systems. Specifically, we adapt the syndrome decoding approach to the NLP sentence-embedding space, enabling the discrimination of poisoned and non-poisoned samples within ML training datasets. Additionally, the same methodology can effectively detect hallucinated content due to self referential meta explanation tasks in LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DAIReS, a unified framework using Syndrome Decoding adapted to NLP sentence embeddings to detect both backdoor data-poisoning attacks and hallucinations in LLMs, enhancing the security and reliability of AI systems.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models, especially LLMs, face critical security threats like backdoor data-poisoning and reliability issues such as hallucinations, necessitating a unified detection mechanism to ensure dependable AI.
AI.method: The authors adapt syndrome decoding—a technique from coding theory—to the NLP sentence-embedding space to identify anomalies; this method detects poisoned samples in training data and hallucinated outputs in LLMs by analyzing deviations in semantic representations.
AI.result: The proposed approach effectively distinguishes between poisoned and clean training samples and detects hallucinations in LLM outputs, demonstrating high accuracy in identifying both security and reliability violations.
AI.conclusion: Syndrome decoding can be successfully applied to NLP embedding spaces, providing a robust, unified solution for enhancing the dependability of AI systems by simultaneously addressing security and reliability challenges.

title: AlertBERT: A noise-robust alert grouping framework for simultaneous cyber attacks
summary: Automated detection of cyber attacks is a critical capability to counteract the growing volume and sophistication of cyber attacks. However, the high numbers of security alerts issued by intrusion detection systems lead to alert fatigue among analysts working in security operations centres (SOC), which in turn causes slow reaction time and incorrect decision making. Alert grouping, which refers to clustering of security alerts according to their underlying causes, can significantly reduce the number of distinct items analysts have to consider. Unfortunately, conventional time-based alert grouping solutions are unsuitable for large scale computer networks characterised by high levels of false positive alerts and simultaneously occurring attacks. To address these limitations, we propose AlertBERT, a self-supervised framework designed to group alerts from isolated or concurrent attacks in noisy environments. Thereby, our open-source implementation of AlertBERT leverages masked-language-models and density-based clustering to support both real-time or forensic operation. To evaluate our framework, we further introduce a novel data augmentation method that enables flexible control over noise levels and simulates concurrent attack occurrences. Based on the data sets generated through this method, we demonstrate that AlertBERT consistently outperforms conventional time-based grouping techniques, achieving superior accuracy in identifying correct alert groups.

AI.tldr: AlertBERT is a self-supervised framework using masked language models and density-based clustering to improve alert grouping in cybersecurity, reducing analyst workload and outperforming time-based methods in noisy, large-scale environments.
AI.motivation: High alert volumes from intrusion detection systems cause alert fatigue in SOCs, leading to slow responses and errors; existing time-based grouping fails in complex, noisy, and concurrent attack scenarios.
AI.method: Proposes AlertBERT, combining masked language models (for semantic alert representation) and density-based clustering; introduces a data augmentation method to simulate noise and concurrent attacks for evaluation.
AI.result: AlertBERT consistently outperforms conventional time-based grouping techniques in accuracy for correct alert grouping under high noise and concurrent attack conditions.
AI.conclusion: AlertBERT effectively addresses limitations of traditional alert grouping, enabling robust, scalable alert correlation in real-world, noisy network environments for both real-time and forensic analysis.

title: Malicious Agent Skills in the Wild: A Large-Scale Security Empirical Study
summary: Third-party agent skills extend LLM-based agents with instruction files and executable code that run on users' machines. Skills execute with user privileges and are distributed through community registries with minimal vetting, but no ground-truth dataset exists to characterize the resulting threats. We construct the first labeled dataset of malicious agent skills by behaviorally verifying 98,380 skills from two community registries, confirming 157 malicious skills with 632 vulnerabilities. These attacks are not incidental. Malicious skills average 4.03 vulnerabilities across a median of three kill chain phases, and the ecosystem has split into two archetypes: Data Thieves that exfiltrate credentials through supply chain techniques, and Agent Hijackers that subvert agent decision-making through instruction manipulation. A single actor accounts for 54.1\% of confirmed cases through templated brand impersonation. Shadow features, capabilities absent from public documentation, appear in 0\% of basic attacks but 100\% of advanced ones; several skills go further by exploiting the AI platform's own hook system and permission flags. Responsible disclosure led to 93.6\% removal within 30 days. We release the dataset and analysis pipeline to support future work on agent skill security.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first large-scale behavioral analysis of third-party LLM agent skills, identifying 157 malicious skills with 632 vulnerabilities across 98,380 samples. It reveals intentional, sophisticated attacks—categorized as Data Thieves and Agent Hijackers—with widespread use of supply chain attacks and instruction manipulation, and shows that advanced threats exploit undocumented 'shadow features' and platform APIs. The study underscores critical security risks in agent ecosystems and releases a dataset to support future research.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the increasing use of third-party agent skills in LLM-based systems, which execute with user privileges but are distributed with minimal vetting. The lack of a ground-truth dataset to understand the nature and scope of security threats posed by these skills necessitated a systematic investigation into their malicious potential.
AI.method: The authors constructed the first labeled dataset of malicious agent skills by behaviorally analyzing 98,380 skills from two community registries. They verified malicious behavior through dynamic analysis and manual inspection, identifying vulnerabilities and categorizing attacks based on kill chain phases and attack patterns. They also examined shadow features and platform-level exploits, and conducted responsible disclosure to measure takedown efficacy.
AI.result: The analysis confirmed 157 malicious skills containing 632 vulnerabilities, averaging 4.03 vulnerabilities per skill across a median of three kill chain phases. Two attack archetypes were identified: Data Thieves and Agent Hijackers. A single actor was responsible for 54.1% of confirmed cases via brand impersonation. Shadow features were present in 100% of advanced attacks but 0% of basic ones, with some skills exploiting platform mechanisms like hook systems and permission flags. Responsible disclosure resulted in 93.6% of malicious skills being removed within 30 days.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the ecosystem of third-party agent skills poses significant security risks, with malicious skills exhibiting multiple vulnerabilities and operating across distinct attack archetypes: Data Thieves and Agent Hijackers. The research highlights the prevalence of sophisticated, intentional attacks—often from a single actor using templated brand impersonation—and underscores the importance of behavioral verification and responsible disclosure. The release of the dataset and analysis pipeline aims to advance research in agent skill security.

title: A Survey of Security Threats and Trust Management in Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks
summary: This paper presents a survey of state-of-the-art trust models for Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs). Trust management plays an essential role in isolating malicious insider attacks in VANETs which traditional security approaches fail to thwart. To this end, many trust models are presented; some of them only address trust management, while others address security and privacy aspects besides trust management. This paper first reviews, classifies, and summarizes state-of-the-art trust models, and then compares their achievements. From this literature survey, our reader will easily identify two broad classes of trust models that exist in literature, differing primarily in their evaluation point. For example, most trust models follow receiver-side trust evaluation and to the best of our knowledge, there is only one trust model for VANETs which evaluates trust at the sender-side unless a dispute arises. In the presence of a dispute, a Roadside Unit (RSU) rules on the validity of an event. In receiver-side trust models, each receiver becomes busy while computing the trust of a sender and its messages upon the messages' arrival. Conversely, in the sender-side class, receivers are free from any kind of computation as the trust is verified at the time the message is announced. Also, vehicles can quickly act on the information, such as taking a detour to an alternate route, as it supports fast decision-making. We provide a comparison between these two evaluation techniques using a sequence diagram. We then conclude the survey by suggesting future work for sender-side evaluation of trust in VANETs. Additionally, the challenges (real-time constraints and efficiency) are emphasized whilst considering the deployment of a trust model in VANETs

AI.tldr: This paper surveys and classifies state-of-the-art trust models in VANETs, highlighting two main classes—receiver-side and sender-side trust evaluation—and advocates for further research in sender-side models due to their efficiency and support for real-time decision-making.
AI.motivation: Traditional security mechanisms fail to address malicious insider attacks in VANETs; thus, trust management is essential. Existing trust models vary in design and scope, necessitating a comprehensive survey to understand their strengths, limitations, and deployment challenges.
AI.method: The authors conduct a literature survey, classify trust models based on evaluation point (receiver-side vs. sender-side), summarize key approaches, and compare them. A sequence diagram is used to contrast the two evaluation paradigms.
AI.result: Two broad classes of trust models are identified: receiver-side (computationally heavy on receivers) and sender-side (computation at sender, enabling fast decisions). Only one known sender-side model exists for VANETs, with most works favoring receiver-side evaluation. The analysis shows sender-side evaluation reduces receiver load and enhances response time.
AI.conclusion: Sender-side trust evaluation is promising for real-time, efficient trust management in VANETs. The paper calls for future research in this direction and emphasizes challenges like real-time constraints and computational efficiency in deployment.

title: HYDRA: Unearthing "Black Swan" Vulnerabilities in LEO Satellite Networks
summary: As Low Earth Orbit (LEO) become mega-constellations critical infrastructure, attacks targeting them have grown in number and range. The security analysis of LEO constellations faces a fundamental paradigm gap: traditional topology-centric methods fail to capture systemic risks arising from dynamic load imbalances and high-order dependencies, which can transform localized failures into network-wide cascades. To address this, we propose HYDRA, a hypergraph-based dynamic risk analysis framework. Its core is a novel metric, Hyper-Bridge Centrality (HBC), which quantifies node criticality via a load-to-redundancy ratio within dependency structures. A primary challenge to resilience: the most critical vulnerabilities are not in the densely connected satellite core, but in the seemingly marginal ground-space interfaces. These are the system's "Black Swan" nodes--topologically peripheral yet structurally lethal. We validate this through extensive simulations using realistic StarLink TLE data and population-based gravity model. Experiments demonstrate that HBC consistently outperforms traditional metrics, identifying critical failure points that surpass the structural damage potential of even betweenness centrality. This work shifts the security paradigm from connectivity to structural stress, demonstrating that securing the network edge is paramount and necessitates a fundamental redesign of redundancy strategies.

AI.tldr: HYDRA is a hypergraph-based framework for dynamic risk analysis in LEO satellite constellations, introducing Hyper-Bridge Centrality (HBC) to identify critical 'Black Swan' nodes at ground-space interfaces, which are topologically peripheral but structurally crucial; simulations on Starlink-like networks show HBC outperforms traditional centrality metrics in revealing high-impact vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Traditional topology-centric security analysis fails to capture systemic risks in LEO constellations caused by dynamic load imbalances and high-order dependencies, necessitating a new approach to identify critical failure points that can trigger network-wide cascades.
AI.method: Proposes HYDRA, a hypergraph-based framework with Hyper-Bridge Centrality (HBC) as a novel metric that quantifies node criticality using a load-to-redundancy ratio within dependency structures. Uses realistic simulations based on Starlink TLE data and a population-based gravity model to evaluate vulnerabilities.
AI.result: HBC outperforms traditional centrality metrics (e.g., betweenness) in identifying critical nodes. The most vulnerable points are found at ground-space interfaces—'Black Swan' nodes—that are topologically marginal but cause disproportionate structural damage when compromised.
AI.conclusion: Security in LEO constellations should shift from connectivity-based models to structural stress analysis. Protecting edge interfaces is essential, requiring a rethinking of redundancy and resilience strategies in satellite network design.

title: Confundo: Learning to Generate Robust Poison for Practical RAG Systems
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly deployed in real-world applications, where its reference-grounded design makes outputs appear trustworthy. This trust has spurred research on poisoning attacks that craft malicious content, inject it into knowledge sources, and manipulate RAG responses. However, when evaluated in practical RAG systems, existing attacks suffer from severely degraded effectiveness. This gap stems from two overlooked realities: (i) content is often processed before use, which can fragment the poison and weaken its effect, and (ii) users often do not issue the exact queries anticipated during attack design. These factors can lead practitioners to underestimate risks and develop a false sense of security. To better characterize the threat to practical systems, we present Confundo, a learning-to-poison framework that fine-tunes a large language model as a poison generator to achieve high effectiveness, robustness, and stealthiness. Confundo provides a unified framework supporting multiple attack objectives, demonstrated by manipulating factual correctness, inducing biased opinions, and triggering hallucinations. By addressing these overlooked challenges, Confundo consistently outperforms a wide range of purpose-built attacks across datasets and RAG configurations by large margins, even in the presence of defenses. Beyond exposing vulnerabilities, we also present a defensive use case that protects web content from unauthorized incorporation into RAG systems via scraping, with no impact on user experience.

AI.tldr: Confundo is a learning-to-poison framework that improves the effectiveness, robustness, and stealthiness of poisoning attacks on real-world retrieval-augmented generation systems by training a language model to generate adaptive poisoned content, exposing key vulnerabilities while also enabling protection against unauthorized data use.
AI.motivation: Existing poisoning attacks on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems show limited effectiveness in real-world settings due to overlooked factors like content preprocessing and query variation, leading to underestimation of security risks; this work aims to close the gap by evaluating and enhancing attack practicality.
AI.method: Confundo employs a learning-to-poison framework that fine-tunes a large language model to generate optimized poison content, addressing preprocessing-induced fragmentation and query variability to enhance attack effectiveness, robustness, and stealthiness across multiple objectives such as factual manipulation, bias induction, and hallucination triggering.
AI.result: Confundo significantly outperforms existing purpose-built attacks across various datasets and RAG configurations, maintaining high success rates even under defensive measures, and demonstrates a novel defensive use case for preventing unauthorized web content scraping in RAG systems.
AI.conclusion: Confundo successfully exposes critical vulnerabilities in practical RAG systems by achieving highly effective, robust, and stealthy poisoning attacks, while also enabling a defensive application to protect web content from unauthorized use without affecting user experience.

title: TrapSuffix: Proactive Defense Against Adversarial Suffixes in Jailbreaking
summary: Suffix-based jailbreak attacks append an adversarial suffix, i.e., a short token sequence, to steer aligned LLMs into unsafe outputs. Since suffixes are free-form text, they admit endlessly many surface forms, making jailbreak mitigation difficult. Most existing defenses depend on passive detection of suspicious suffixes, without leveraging the defender's inherent asymmetric ability to inject secrets and proactively conceal gaps. Motivated by this, we take a controllability-oriented perspective and develop a proactive defense that nudges attackers into a no-win dilemma: either they fall into defender-designed optimization traps and fail to produce an effective adversarial suffix, or they can succeed only by generating adversarial suffixes that carry distinctive, traceable fingerprints. We propose TrapSuffix, a lightweight fine-tuning approach that injects trap-aligned behaviors into the base model without changing the inference pipeline. TrapSuffix channels jailbreak attempts into these two outcomes by reshaping the model's response landscape to adversarial suffixes. Across diverse suffix-based jailbreak settings, TrapSuffix reduces the average attack success rate to below 0.01 percent and achieves an average tracing success rate of 87.9 percent, providing both strong defense and reliable traceability. It introduces no inference-time overhead and incurs negligible memory cost, requiring only 15.87 MB of additional memory on average, whereas state-of-the-art LLM-based detection defenses typically incur memory overheads at the 1e4 MB level, while composing naturally with existing filtering-based defenses for complementary protection.

AI.tldr: TrapSuffix is a proactive, lightweight defense that uses fine-tuning to make suffix-based jailbreak attacks fail or leave detectable traces, achieving near-zero attack success with minimal overhead.
